standard.title: Vocabulary choices for topic
standard.description: experiment with and begin to make conscious choices of vocabulary to suit the topic
standard.prior_knowledge: Students recognise vocabulary associated with different learning area topics (AC9E1LA09). They have not yet experimented with making conscious vocabulary choices — replacing everyday language with topic-specific alternatives.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can experiment with vocabulary choices to suit a topic, making conscious decisions to select topic-specific language over everyday alternatives.

nodes.label: Everyday language vs topic-specific language
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify that topic-specific vocabulary is more precise than everyday language for communicating about a topic, and give at least one example.
nodes.minimum_width: Replace an everyday word with a topic-specific alternative in a given sentence (e.g. replacing 'went' with 'migrated' in a science text).
nodes.typical_width: Identify topic-specific vocabulary in learning area texts, discuss why it is more precise than everyday alternatives, and practise selecting topic-specific vocabulary across Science, HASS and English contexts.
wider: Compare the same information written using everyday language vs topic-specific vocabulary and discuss the difference in precision and audience expectations

Identify First Nations Australians' language words relevant to a specific topic (e.g. Country-related vocabulary in an environmental topic) and discuss what they communicate that everyday language does not

response_modes.reason: Students often perceive everyday language as 'normal' and topic-specific language as 'hard words'. Multiple subject-area contexts — each with their own topic vocabulary — help students see that specificity is purposeful and reader-serving, not an arbitrary difficulty increase. Cross-curriculum examples are the productive move.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations Australians' language words relevant to a topic offer a genuinely enriching direction — they demonstrate that topic-specific vocabulary can carry cultural knowledge that no English equivalent does. This is meaningful enrichment, not just more examples.
success_criteria: Student can replace at least one everyday word with a topic-specific alternative and explain why the specific word is more precise.
Student can identify topic-specific vocabulary in a given text and name the topic it belongs to.

nodes.label: Vocabulary for character description
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can select specific nouns and adjectives to describe characters in narratives, moving beyond generic terms to precise vocabulary.
nodes.minimum_width: Replace a generic character description word ('wizard') with a more specific alternative or compare two specific terms ('magician', 'sorcerer', 'wizard') and discuss the difference.
nodes.typical_width: Explore vocabulary for character description in narratives — distinguishing between synonymous nouns and adjectives and selecting the most precise for a given character and context.
wider: Compare how different authors describe similar character types (e.g. powerful figures, children in danger) and identify the vocabulary choices that create distinct impressions
Experiment with changing one or two vocabulary choices in a character description and discuss how the impression of the character shifts
success_criteria: Student can select a specific noun or adjective for a character and explain what impression it creates.
Student can distinguish between two near-synonyms (e.g. 'timid' vs 'frightened') and explain the different impression each creates.

nodes.label: Making conscious vocabulary choices
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can make conscious vocabulary choices when writing — experimenting with alternatives and selecting the word that best suits the topic and purpose.
nodes.minimum_width: In a short piece of writing, identify one vocabulary choice they made deliberately and explain why they chose that word over an alternative.
nodes.typical_width: During editing, make at least two deliberate vocabulary replacements — replacing everyday language with topic-specific or more precise vocabulary — and explain each choice.
wider: Use a vocabulary journal or word wall from a current topic to draw on topic-specific vocabulary when writing, making choices from the range available
Compare a draft and a revised version of their own writing, annotating the vocabulary changes and explaining the improvement

response_modes.reason: Making a conscious vocabulary choice involves a reasoning chain — what is the topic, who is the audience, what does this word mean vs this one, which is more precise? Making that reasoning explicit (through think-aloud, annotation or discussion) helps students internalise the process rather than defaulting to the first word that comes to mind.

nodes.hinge_reason: Without an explicit reasoning process for vocabulary selection, students default to the first word available throughout all writing — the conscious choice-making habit established here is required for the editing phase in any subsequent writing task.
success_criteria: Student can identify and explain at least one deliberate vocabulary choice in their own writing.
Student replaces at least one everyday word with a topic-specific or more precise alternative during editing.
